data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"Popper's preference for the better-corroborated theory is defensible on his own terms not as an inductive prediction of future success, but as a methodological rule for maximizing 'verisimilitude' (truth-likeness) and minimizing known error, accepting that this offers no guarantee against future falsification but represents the most rational non-probabilistic stance available.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If preferring Theory A over B based on past tests logically entails assuming the future will resemble the past, then the distinction collapses into induction.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If Popper's formal definition of verisimilitude is logically incoherent (as argued by Tich\u00fd and Miller), then it cannot serve as the basis for rational preference.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory inherently implies an expectation of its future reliability, then any claim of avoiding induction is merely semantic.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The argument distinguishes between 'justification' (which requires induction) and 'critical preference' (which relies on the logical asymmetry of falsification). By treating corroboration as a report of past performance rather than a probability score, the scientist chooses the theory that has withstood the severest tests because it contains more empirical content and has survived attempts to refute it. This choice is a bet on truth-likeness, not a calculation of future frequency. The cost of this position is the acceptance of 'rational ignorance': we act on the best theory knowing it may be false tomorrow, without the comfort of assigning it a high probability of being true.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
